data.name: Maze Trials
data.detailed_description:
The Labyrinth is infinite, and it calls to you.

Dive headfirst into a new, procedurally generated maze every time you play. These aren't just simple puzzles; they are sprawling, complex worlds of winding corridors and dead ends, stretching up to a massive 7000x5700 in size. Your only goal is to find the exit. But escape is temporary, leading only to another, more daunting challenge.

Before each descent, you are granted a five-second overview—a fleeting chance to plot your course. Armed with the ability to place markers, you must navigate the twisting paths, collect valuable coins, and race against the clock. As the minutes tick by, the pressure mounts. Can you find the portal before you are lost forever?

Features:

  • Truly Endless Mazes: With procedural generation, no two runs are ever the same. A new challenge awaits you every single time.

  • Massive, Sprawling Scale: Navigate colossal mazes that will test your memory and sense of direction to their absolute limits.

  • Strategic Gameplay: Use the 5-second overview to find a potential path and place markers to track your progress, mark intersections, or signal dead ends.

  • Race Against the Clock: A persistent timer tracks your performance on each level. The longer you take, the more intense it gets.

  • Track Your Progress: A save system automatically records your total mazes completed, coins collected.

  • Atmospheric Experience: A dynamic soundtrack sets the mood for your tense, solitary journey.

The Labyrinth awaits. How many levels can you conquer?

data.short_description: Master an endless descent into massive, procedurally generated mazes. Use markers to find your way, collect coins, and race the clock to find the portal. Each exit only leads to a new labyrinth. It's a pure test of navigation and endurance—how deep can you go?

reviews.review:
Maze Trials is a very simple game, but I think the idea works because it knows exactly what it wants me to do. I am dropped into a huge procedurally generated maze and given one job, find the exit before the timer runs out. Before each maze starts, I get a few seconds to look at the layout and try to remember where I might need to go. After that I am on my own, running through corridors, taking wrong turns and trying to keep my bearings. There is no combat or story to distract me, so the whole game is about navigation.

The maze design is what makes it interesting for me. The layouts are generated each time, and some of them can be extremely large, so I cannot just memorise one fixed map and repeat it. I can place markers while I explore, which is really useful when I reach an important junction or find a dead end. I like this because the markers become part of my way of thinking about the maze. I am not just blindly wandering around. I am trying to build a mental map and leave myself useful clues as I go.

The timer adds most of the pressure. I can take my time to work things out, but every wrong turn costs me more seconds and makes the eventual search harder. I like the tension when I know I am close to the exit but I am not completely sure where I am. At the same time, the timer can make the game feel frustrating when I am clearly searching the right area but keep hitting dead ends. There is a balance between careful navigation and moving quickly, and learning when to stop second guessing myself is a big part of getting better.

There is also a simple progression system through coins and completed mazes. Coins can be collected along the way, while the game keeps track of how many mazes I have finished. There are 11 achievements as well, which gives me some extra goals when I want to push further. I like having these little things to work towards, although they do not completely change the main gameplay. I am still doing the same thing each time, just trying to get deeper into the labyrinth and become better at finding my way around.

The biggest weakness is that the concept can become repetitive quite quickly. Procedural generation means the layouts change, but I am still walking through corridors and looking for a portal. Once the initial challenge of learning how the system works wears off, there are not many new mechanics waiting for me. The game also has a very basic presentation, which fits the simple idea but does not give me much reason to explore beyond the maze itself. The soundtrack helps create a lonely atmosphere, but I would have liked a few more ideas to break up the repeated navigation.

I also think Maze Trials works much better in short sessions than as something I play for hours. I can run a maze, see how far I get, take a break and come back later without needing to remember a story or complicated progression system. The endless structure gives it a nice pick up and play quality, and I like that each attempt can feel different simply because I have no idea what the next layout is going to look like. Still, the lack of variety means I eventually reach a point where I feel like I have already seen everything the game is offering, even though the actual mazes are different.

Overall, Maze Trials is a decent little navigation game that gets a surprising amount of tension out of a very basic idea. I like the massive procedural mazes, short planning period, marker system and constant pressure from the timer. The lack of combat, story and deeper progression keeps the experience limited, and the repetition becomes noticeable after enough runs. For me, it works best as a simple challenge I can pick up for a while rather than a game I would spend a huge amount of time with. It has a clear identity and does what it sets out to do, but it needs more variety to reach the higher end of my ratings.

Rating: 7.2/10
